myndigheter.071: 252 agencies from Statistics Sweden's register of government agencies. Agencies that share an email domain are measured once, so the table has one row per domain.
myndigheter.072: The Swedish Tax Agency shows what the measurement cannot see
myndigheter.073: According to Swedish Radio's Ekot, the Swedish Tax Agency (Skatteverket) has adopted US cloud services on a large scale. Yet DNS shows email without cloud signals and the website makes no third-party requests. Microsoft's own email configuration service responds that the domain is registered in Exchange Online. 58 agency domains that do not appear as Microsoft in DNS are registered there. Absence of signals is not absence of cloud.

fynd.103: Almost all municipalities have their domain registered in Microsoft's email service
fynd.105: In DNS, email points to Microsoft at 245 municipalities and regions: at 189, Microsoft receives the email according to the MX record, and at 56 a spam filter or their own server comes first but SPF and DKIM or autodiscover are configured for Microsoft. The latter show configuration, not where the email actually ends up. Sollentuna, Norrköping and Halmstad are configured for both Microsoft and Google.
fynd.106: Microsoft's own email configuration service also responds that the domain is registered in an Exchange Online organisation for 305 of 310, including all 32 where DNS was not enough, 19 of 20 without cloud signals in DNS and 7 of 10 that receive email at Google. Among agency domains, this applies to 142 of 202, the Swedish Tax Agency included. The registration does not show that email is received or stored there; that 7 of 10 Google municipalities answer yes shows the limit.
fynd.108: The checks test different parts of the measurement chain and share some of it: the email class was queried via three other DNS resolvers (512 of 512 identical; same records and same rules, so this tests the resolvers, not the rules), Microsoft accounts via a second Microsoft endpoint (512 of 512), the networks behind third-party hosts via RIPEstat (338 of 338 same ASN; this tests the registry, not which address the browser used). The Exchange Online check first failed its requirement because of a bug in our code and throttling; after the correction, 331 of 333 among those classified as Microsoft. A later run from GitHub Actions did not meet the requirement and is not published. Only yes or no is stored.
fynd.112: At half of the municipalities, no service names were found on US networks
fynd.114: Certificate logs show names under an organisation's domain that have been issued a certificate: e-services, booking, login pages, websites and the like. At 150 of 289 municipalities, no such name was found with an address on a US network; the median per municipality is 0 %. This does not mean the municipality has no US services: names without their own certificate, services on the provider's domain and names covered only by wildcard certificates are not visible.
fynd.115: Counting all names, 15.7 % of the municipalities' 5,342 names are on US networks, including CDNs such as Cloudflare, but the total is driven by a few: a single municipality accounts for 25 % of the municipalities' names on US networks. Regions are higher: 19 of 20 have at least one name on a US network and the median is 13 %. Among agency domains the median is 3 %. Of all names, most are on networks owned by European companies, 14 on networks in other countries and 16 on networks that could not be identified; the measurement does not say where the servers are located.
fynd.116: The names come from crt.sh, with Certspotter as a fallback. A name counts if it has a public IPv4 address at the time of measurement; that does not show a service actually runs there. Names pointing to internal addresses (1,268 in total) are not counted, and the number is stored only as a total. No hostnames are stored or published. The first run failed the requirement for the share of names with a known network and was never published.
fynd.117: For comparison, 20 randomly selected organisations were also measured with the second source: the share differed by at most 15 percentage points for 18 of 20 (requirement 16). This compares shares, not whether the list of names is complete, and both sources read the same certificate logs. The tolerance is not enough to test the zero category: for Grums the main source found no names on US networks but the second source did. The direction of the error from wildcard certificates and domain selection has not been investigated.
fynd.119: Agency websites call Google before consent
fynd.121: 30 of 193 measurable agency domains made requests to Google Tag Manager or Google Analytics before the visitor had given consent. 11 of them called Google Analytics servers, where visitor statistics are received; the other 19 only called Tag Manager. The Swedish Armed Forces are one of those that load Tag Manager.
fynd.122: The measurement records request attempts in the browser's network log; whether the request succeeded is not stored. The Swedish Armed Forces were checked in a regular Chrome without a consent cookie: googletagmanager.com/gtm.js was in the browser's resource list, so it was loaded, but there were no requests to Google Analytics. A successful request to Tag Manager gives Google the visitor's IP address and browser information; it does not mean visitor statistics are collected.
fynd.125: Sixteen municipalities call Google Analytics or Tag Manager before consent
fynd.127: Eleven municipalities' pages made requests to Google Analytics servers, where visitor statistics are received, while the cookie banner was still unanswered: Valdemarsvik, Emmaboda, Borgholm, Hässleholm, Dals-Ed, Färgelanda, Mellerud, Åmål, Norsjö, Storuman and Pajala.
fynd.128: Five only called Google Tag Manager, without any request to Google Analytics: Jönköping, Oskarshamn, Sölvesborg, Vänersborg and Sunne. A successful Tag Manager request gives Google the IP address and browser information but does not by itself collect visitor statistics.
fynd.129: Hässleholm's request contains a parameter suggesting Google's Consent Mode, where cookieless requests are sent before consent. Whether that complies with the rules is not decided here.
fynd.130: Headless Chrome with a network log, no button clicked. The log shows request attempts; whether the request succeeded is not stored. In a regular Chrome, Hässleholm's request reached Google Analytics, which responded (HTTP 503), and Tag Manager loaded for Jönköping and Sunne. Before each run we check that a blank page gives zero hits and that a page with Google Analytics gives a hit. All sixteen were measured again on 9 October with the same result.
fynd.132: The cookie banner itself is often loaded from a US network
fynd.134: At 31 municipalities and regions, the page calls the consent tool, the box where the visitor chooses whether data may be sent, on a server in a US company's network. Cookiebot is reached via Akamai (9), Cookie-Script via DigitalOcean (8), Cookie Information via Microsoft (5), and Cookie Tractor, CookieYes, Klaro and OneTrust via Cloudflare. A consent tool has to load before the visitor can answer; the finding concerns where it is loaded from.
fynd.135: For eleven of them, the cookie banner is the only contact with a US network before the visitor has chosen anything.
fynd.136: Each third-party host was looked up to its network (ASN) at the time of measurement. Which domains count as consent tools is defined in fynd_siffror.py. That a tool is fetched from a US network does not say where the tool's own servers and databases are.
fynd.138: The read-aloud service is the second most common on US networks
fynd.140: After Google (76), Texthelp's read-aloud service BrowseAloud, which reads the page aloud for those who need it, is the service most often called on a US network before consent. It is reached via Amazon CloudFront. It is an accessibility tool, not ad tracking.
fynd.141: The addresses were compared with Amazon's published list of IP addresses: they belong to CloudFront, a CDN with servers all over the world. The visitor is probably served by a server in Europe. Where Texthelp's own servers are located is not visible from the outside.
fynd.142: Twenty made no third-party requests before consent
fynd.144: Upplands Väsby, Huddinge, Eskilstuna, Trosa, Malmö, Landskrona, Eslöv, Trelleborg, Simrishamn, Partille, Orust, Gullspång, Filipstad, Gävle, Sundsvall, Ragunda, Vindeln, Övertorneå, Älvsbyn and Region Stockholm load everything from their own website before the visitor has answered. Two of them, Partille and Region Stockholm, have the website itself behind Cloudflare, a US CDN.
fynd.145: Huddinge was checked in a regular Chrome with an unanswered cookie banner: all 31 resources were fetched from www.huddinge.se.
fynd.147: Google receives, DKIM published at Microsoft
fynd.149: Ödeshög, Ydre, Boxholm, Åtvidaberg and Vimmerby receive email at Google but have published DKIM keys at Microsoft. This suggests email is sent via Microsoft, but whether it is actually signed there was not checked; the keys may also be left over. Four of them are in Östergötland, where five of fourteen receive email at Google.
fynd.150: dig +short MX atvidaberg.se points to Google; dig +short CNAME selector1._domainkey.atvidaberg.se points to Microsoft. All five were checked again on 9 October.
fynd.151: One in three municipalities has DMARC in monitoring mode
fynd.153: DMARC is a DNS record where the domain owner tells receivers what to do with email that claims to come from the domain but fails the check. 97 municipalities and regions have p=none: they ask for reports but not for such email to be stopped; receivers then only apply their own filters. 132 have p=reject. 34 have published MTA-STS, which can prevent email to them from being sent unencrypted; whether the policy is actually enforced was not checked. DNSSEC is in place at 257.
fynd.154: The lookups were made via 1.1.1.1. The DNS signals were repeated via 9.9.9.9: 510–512 of 512 identical per signal. DNS errors count as errors, not as missing records, and a run with more than 2 % errors is not published. The result is reported only per county, and counties with fewer than five organisations are merged, never per organisation.
fynd.157: All but one have a Microsoft account
fynd.159: All municipalities and regions except Gällivare have a Microsoft Entra tenant on the measured domain. Gällivare has one on its other domain, gallivare.se. An account does not say how much it is used.
fynd.160: Microsoft's public OpenID address responds 200 for a domain with a tenant and 400 without. Checked against benbo.se and a made-up domain, both of which gave 400.
fynd.161: The Swedish Tax Agency barely shows up in the measurement, and that is a finding
fynd.162: According to Ekot (Swedish Radio), the Swedish Tax Agency (Skatteverket) has adopted US cloud services on a large scale. In DNS, the agency has email on its own servers without cloud signals, and in the measurement the website made no third-party requests. What is visible is a Microsoft account and that the domain is registered in Exchange Online.
fynd.163: It shows how little can be seen from the outside. The measurements concern configuration and requests visible from the internet, not how dependent an organisation is on US clouds. Services used internally leave few traces.
fynd.165: We measured ourselves: US cloud, but no third parties
fynd.166: Molnkartan runs on GitHub Pages, which is owned by Microsoft and delivered via Fastly. The DNS measurements run every month in GitHub Actions on Microsoft's Azure; the web measurement is made from Sweden. With the same tools as for the municipalities: the site makes no third-party requests and sets no cookies, but the hosting is on a US network.
fynd.167: The difference from a municipality is that the site does not handle personal data or exercise public authority. But we do not want to claim anything about others that we do not say about ourselves.
fynd.170: Errors that we and our reviewers have found in the method, with dates. Nothing is rewritten afterwards; see also How it was made.
fynd.172: A reviewer from another AI model found that we claimed too much
fynd.173: After our own reviews, we had Codex, a model from another company, review the whole project. It found errors our reviewers missed, because they were based on the same model as us. The most important:
fynd.174: The web measurement records request attempts in the browser's network log, not that contact succeeded. The findings said "contacts".
fynd.175: The Microsoft classification of email rests on different kinds of evidence: MX for most, but only published configuration (SPF, DKIM) for some. This is now reported separately.
fynd.176: The checks were called independent although several share a source or classification with the main measurement. Each check now describes what it can detect.
fynd.177: "Half of the municipalities have no services on US networks" was a claim of absence the measurement cannot support, and the check passed a case where the second source found US names.
fynd.178: That all numbers are "lower bounds" was not established for every measure, and the project's question about "dependence" is not measured directly.
fynd.179: In some failures (DNS timeout, Chrome crash, incomplete pagination) the code could silently give a negative answer instead of "could not be measured". No published numbers have been shown to be affected, and it is fixed: such failures now become "could not be measured".
fynd.180: All points are issues on GitHub with Codex's counter-examples.
fynd.181: An independent review found errors in our findings
fynd.182: Before sharing the site, we had a separate reviewer, who had not built the project and only had read access, try to disprove each finding against the raw data. Among other things, it found:
fynd.183: that the Google Analytics headline was wrong for five municipalities that only load Tag Manager,
fynd.184: that the Exchange Online finding claimed more than the measurement shows,
fynd.185: that the number with a consent tool on a US network was 31, not 28,
fynd.186: that two automatic runs that failed their requirements had been published anyway,
fynd.187: that DMARC p=none was described incorrectly, and
fynd.188: that Gotland County, with a single organisation, revealed individual values although the security basics are only to be reported in groups.
fynd.189: Everything is corrected on this page. Runs that fail their requirements are no longer published, and every number here is checked automatically against the raw data.
fynd.190: Two tests failed before the website measurement held
fynd.191: The website rules were tested on counties they were not built on. A hand-written list of providers missed 51 % of the hosts in Skåne and 28 % in Västra Götaland, against the requirement of 10 %. No classifications from those runs were published. Version 3 classifies by the network behind each host and met the coverage requirement on Norrland, with a known network for 99 % of hosts. That measures that the classification can be made, not that it is right. Hässleholm's Google Analytics requests were discovered in the Skåne run and then confirmed separately.
fynd.193: The animation found an error in our rules
fynd.195: The animation on the home page replays the measurement with real responses. For Åtvidaberg it showed a DKIM response that clearly pointed to Microsoft, while the signal said "none". The rule only recognised Microsoft's older format. After the correction, Gotland, Sjöbo and Bromölla changed from "could not be determined" to Microsoft. The correction is dated in the method, and the old numbers remain.

om.202: The cloud character, with a magnifying glass
om.203: Molnkartan was built by Reda Ekengren together with Claude Code, an AI agent from Anthropic. Claude wrote the code, ran the measurements and wrote the texts. Reda asked the question, set the rules and decided what could be published.
om.204: An AI is fast, and just as fast at fooling itself
om.205: An agent can measure 512 domains in a few minutes. It can also find the patterns it wants to see, pick the explanation that sounds best and write a headline that claims more than the data. That is why the project is built on rules that make it hard to be wrong without anyone noticing.
om.206: The rules are written before the data. Every classification is in METOD.md (in Swedish), dated, before the measurement runs. If a rule is changed afterwards, it becomes a new version with a new test.
om.207: Tested on data the rules have not seen. Stockholm County was used to develop the rules and Skåne decided whether they held. The web rules failed that test twice and were rewritten before anything was published.
om.208: Independent checks. Every conclusion is tested with another method, for example Microsoft's own answer about a domain, three different DNS services and two sources for which country a network belongs to.
om.209: Reviewers looking for errors. Two separate Claude agents and then Codex from OpenAI were tasked with finding errors. They found several, see the findings about the review.
om.210: Gates before publishing. A measurement that does not reach 95 % coverage, or where the checks fail, is not published. The numbers on the pages are checked by tests against the raw data.
om.211: Ask for the ground truth. In October 2026, 43 municipalities and regions were asked which email service they use, without being told what Molnkartan says about them. The result will be reported here, even if it shows the method was wrong.
om.212: Corrections stay. Errors that are found are dated in the method. Nothing is rewritten afterwards.
om.214: Everything is based on what anyone can see from the outside: DNS, certificate logs and what a web page calls. No logins, no leaks. Names of internal systems and login pages are never published, and security weaknesses are reported only per county.
om.217: What can be seen from the outside of US cloud services at Sweden's 290 municipalities, 20 regions and 202 government agency domains: email via DNS, Microsoft accounts, which networks the website calls before the visitor has given consent, and service names in certificate logs.
om.218: Does Microsoft in the email setup mean the data is stored in the USA?
om.219: No. The measurement shows configuration and requests visible from the internet, not where information is stored, which agreements apply or how dependent the organisation is.
om.220: How do you know the measurement is right?
om.221: The rules are written before the data is collected and tested on a region they were not developed on. Conclusions are checked with independent methods, reviewers have looked for errors, and 43 municipalities and regions have been asked which email service they use.
om.222: How often is the data updated?
om.223: The measurement runs automatically on the 1st of every month. Runs that do not meet their requirements are not published.
om.225: Yes. The data is free to use under CC BY 4.0 and the code under the MIT licence. Everything is on GitHub.
om.227: Reda Ekengren, who built the project together with the AI agent Claude Code from Anthropic. Molnkartan is an independent project, not a government body.
